newsitem.title: GERMANY: Unions, politicians attack banks on German steel merger.
newsitem.headline: Unions, politicians attack banks on German steel merger.

text.p: German trade unions and opposition politicians Tuesday turned the full force of their anger on the banks that supported a rare, but abortive, hostile takeover bid between Germany's two rival steel producers.

Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp Monday dropped plans for a bank-financed takeover of Thyssen AG. Those plans sparked protests from workers and observers, fearful that Germany's consensus economics were being sacrificed to naked capitalism.

The decision did not pacify 30,000 steelworkers who demonstrated at the headquarters of Deutsche Bank in the financial capital, Frankfurt, with banners reading "Deutsche Bank, executioner of the steelworker."
The firms have agreed to form a steel production joint venture to be managed by Thyssen and explore other forms of cooperation short of merger.
The agreement meant Krupp would not have to call on the 15 billion mark ($8.9 billion) credit line it had secured from Deutsche Bank, Dresdner Bank and others.

The banks say they did not instigate the plan but agree they would like to see Germany's steel sector slimmed down to compete with its more efficient British and French rivals -- a process that is still certain to cost thousands of jobs.

Such is the shock to Germany's tradition of consensus among industry, workers, banks and government that the steelworkers have been able to mobilise widespread support among a public increasingly worried by soaring unemployment.

"The banks' machinations are destroying this country's political culture," Klaus Zwickel, head of the engineering union IG Metall, told the demonstrators who had halted production in the steel plants of Duisburg and Dortmund.
Deutsche has come under particular attack because it had directors on the supervisory boards of both firms, but never told Thyssen that it was supporting a takeover by a rival.
"The parties and the parliament have to ask themselves who it is that rules us -- the democratically elected government or the unchecked finance centres of the big banks," Zwickel said.
The opposition Social Democrats joined the attack, urging 5 percent or 10 percent limits on banks' industrial holdings.
Social Democrat financial expert Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier hailed Krupp's climbdown, saying "one of the decisive factors was that banks had to backtrack in the face of the storm of public protest."

With unemployment now at 4.7 million, a level not seen since 1933, Germany's workers have become increasingly afraid of the restructuring of industry and the welfare state that government and economists say is needed to restore German competitiveness.
